title: Bananas (per lb)

drivers.name: Price increase (1.5%)
drivers.evidence: No historical uplift at $0.68; recent week (2026-10-05) sold 388 vs baseline 438.1 (down 11.4%). Noise-adjusted price effect at similar price is near 1.0. A 1.5% increase likely suppresses demand slightly.

drivers.name: Supplier delivery warning
drivers.evidence: Planner note indicates supply risk. No past occurrence of delivery issue, but plausible demand suppression. Risk is uncertain but non-zero. Shrink effect toward 1.0 due to low evidence count.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 438.1. No events or promotions are planned. Price increased 1.5% to $0.68. Recent weeks show no promotion effect at $0.68; sales were 388 (2026-10-05), below baseline. Labor Day (2026-09-07) saw a dip to 241, but no such event this week. Supplier delivery warning introduces supply risk, likely reducing sales. Past price hikes at $0.68 showed no consistent lift; noise-adjusted effect is near 1.0. The 1.5% price increase and delivery risk suggest a downward adjustment. Evidence is thin but directional. Shrink toward 1.0 with caution.

  shelf price: 0.68 (+1.5% vs regular price 0.67)
  planner notes: Supplier warns of a short delivery

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 438.1 | 5%-95%: 313.1 - 555.4 | 10%-90%: 346.9 - 528.6

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-21% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
